findings.title: Closing one strategy shuts down the factory-wide queue pool, so messages are dropped after a rebalance
findings.body: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, and create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (result_consumer.py:255) passes that same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy the factory builds. close() here calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down every queue and stops every worker. join() (line 345) delegates to close(). Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on each partition reassignment, so the new strategy gets an already-shut-down pool. Its submit() then calls FixedQueuePool.submit, which records the offset as outstanding and then queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches that in its broad except, logs 'Error submitting message to queue', and marks the offset complete, so the commit loop advances past it. The net effect is that after the first rebalance every consumed result is silently discarded (only logged) while its offset is still committed. No test creates a second strategy from one factory, so this is not caught. The pool should live for the factory's lifetime and be shut down only in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or each strategy should own its own pool.

findings.title: An offset that never arrives permanently stalls commits for its partition
findings.body: get_committable_offsets walks offsets from last_committed+1 and stops at the first offset that is either outstanding or absent from all_offsets (the else/break at lines 92-93). Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous (log compaction and transaction control markers leave holes). A hole is never added via add_offset, so the loop breaks at it on every cycle and last_committed never advances again for that partition. Everything after the hole keeps accumulating in all_offsets, which mark_committed never prunes, and every one-second commit cycle runs min()/max() over that growing set. Consequences are a frozen committed offset, unbounded consumer lag, and unbounded memory growth. The unit test test_offset_gaps_block_commits only passes because it later submits offset 101 to fill the hole, which a real gap never does. test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps in the results consumer tests asserts the stall as expected behavior.

findings.title: Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure, contrary to the docstring
findings.body: queue.Queue() is created without maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected, so Arroyo never pauses polling. If a worker stalls (a slow result handler or a DB hiccup), every subsequent message is still polled, decoded, and queued, and each WorkItem keeps the full Kafka message alive. Memory grows with the backlog until the process is killed. The class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') is therefore false. Either bound the queues and reject when full, or remove the claim.

findings.title: Docstring promises no item is lost and commits only after success, but failed items are logged and committed
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker.run catches Exception and logs it, and the finally block (line 149) completes the offset anyway, so the offset is committed and the failed result is never retried. The result processor also swallows its own exceptions. The guarantees 'No item is lost' (line 252) and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' (line 254) therefore do not hold. This may match the existing batched modes, but the docstring should not claim otherwise.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the failing batch is NOT committed, contradicting its own docstring
findings.body: The docstring says errors 'don't block offset commits for other messages'. Offsets 100 and 101 both complete: the first raises, the worker logs it and completes the offset in its finally, and the second succeeds. The commit loop should therefore commit 101+1=102 for the partition. The final assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires the opposite. It passes only because the commit thread's first cycle fires about one second after creation while the test checks after roughly 0.2 seconds. On a slower run the commit happens and the test fails. The test should wait for the commit and assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102.

findings.title: Graceful-shutdown test runs the real result processor in worker threads and asserts almost nothing
findings.body: Unlike the other thread-queue tests, this one does not patch result_processor.__call__. The worker threads run the real ResultProcessor, which hits the database through get_from_cache from threads outside the test transaction, and the queued results can still be running after the test returns. The only assertion is factory.queue_pool is None, which does not verify that queued results were processed or that the workers stopped. The processor should be mocked, and the test should assert that all results were handled before shutdown completed and that the worker threads are no longer alive.

findings.title: test_preserves_order_within_group never checks order
findings.body: The test name and docstring claim messages for the same subscription are processed in order, but the only assertion is the count of processed results. Ordering is never checked. Similarly, test_concurrent_processing_different_groups (line 314) does not verify concurrency, only the count. Assert the processed sequence for the group, as the unit test test_ordered_processing_within_group does.

findings.title: test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 after submitting, which races with the workers
findings.body: The workers consume concurrently with the submitting thread, so the queues can be fully drained before get_stats() runs. The assertion `stats["total_items"] > 0` is therefore timing-dependent and can fail intermittently. The check should be dropped or made deterministic, for example by blocking the result processor on an event while the stats are read.

findings.title: Shutdown joins worker threads one after another with 5s timeouts, which can block for about 100s
findings.body: The join loop calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) sequentially for each of the default 20 workers. If workers are still finishing slow items, the worst case is about 5s times the number of queues, all blocking inside close()/join(), which Arroyo invokes on the processing thread during rebalance and shutdown. This can exceed the consumer's poll interval. Use a single shared deadline, or join all workers against one timeout.
